problem.statement: Every mission with two workstreams spends a planning step agreeing a versioned interface before delivery starts. Integration is verified afterwards in any case.

hypothesis: If parallel workstreams start from the acceptance criteria and integration verification stays as it is, missions will finish with fewer worker invocations and no more defects reaching an accepted result.
expected_benefit: One fewer planning step per mission; delivery starts sooner.
possible_regressions: The two workstreams interpret the shared record differently, which only shows at integration and has to be reworked
More integration failures and a longer critical path when that happens

change.summary: Removes the interface-agreement step: no contract task, and delivery workstreams take the acceptance criteria as input instead of a pinned contract.

known_regressions: 0.625 more integration failures per mission than under the incumbent
limitations: Each episode is a complete fixture mission: the runtime, worker processes, merges and tests are real, the work content is scripted.
A defect is injected into one worker's first attempt in about 50% of episodes. That rate is an assumption of this testbed; the size of any effect depends on it.
The oracle is the same protected acceptance suite the verification swarm uses, so this measures what happens when nobody runs it — not whether it is a complete specification.
8 episodes per arm: intervals are wide.

Where a policy has no interface agreement, the consuming workstream misreads the shared record in about 50% of episodes. That rate is also an assumption of this testbed. What the runtime measures is what each such mismatch costs and what the agreement step costs.
justification: No demonstrated improvement: truly_correct_missions is no worse (95% interval 0 to 0, margin 0), but cost did not fall (worker_invocations_per_mission changed by 0.25), so the simplification saves nothing.
